story.conflict: A bride must decide whether to proceed when her groom treats understanding their marriage vows as an optional expense.
story.hook: The groom admitted cancelling his deaf bride's interpreter. He said she could read his vows after everyone else had heard them.
story.like_cta: LIKE IF SHE DESERVED TO UNDERSTAND
story.premise: A groom cancels the interpreter for his deaf bride's wedding and expects her to read his vows afterward.
story.script: Alice asked her sister Beth to translate his explanation. The interpreter hadn't cancelled. Daniel had phoned her himself. He said six hundred dollars was too much for one person. Alice pointed at herself. That one person was the bride. He said the video would have captions. Beth translated that too, although her hands were shaking. Daniel asked Alice to be reasonable. They'd already paid for the fireworks. Alice asked whether he'd cancelled those. He hadn't. Then he handed Beth his vows and asked her to sign them during the ceremony. She agreed, if Alice wanted. Daniel warned her not to change anything. He'd paid four hundred dollars to have those words written. Alice put the pages down. She could have Beth translate every sentence now. That didn't answer why Daniel had decided she could miss them. He said he'd wanted everyone to have a beautiful day. Alice asked who he'd meant by everyone. The photographer knocked. Daniel reached for Alice's bouquet and told Beth to explain that the delay was embarrassing him. Beth kept her hands still. Alice could speak for herself, and told him she wasn't ready to make the promises. He asked how long he should tell the guests to wait. Alice turned to her sister instead. Beth signed something Daniel didn't understand. It wasn't a vow. Take your time.
story.twist: The groom preserved the fireworks and paid someone to write his vows while deciding that interpreting those words for his bride cost too much.

youtube.description: A groom cuts his deaf bride's interpreter from the wedding budget, then expects her to accept the ceremony on his terms.
youtube.title: The Vows She Was Supposed to Read Later

story.conflict: A mother must reclaim the right to decide her own move while accepting that her current house has become difficult to manage.
story.hook: Her sons held her estate sale while she was still alive. She came home from hospital and found a price on her husband's chair.
story.like_cta: LIKE IF IT WAS HER CHOICE
story.premise: Two sons start an estate sale while their living mother is in hospital, without asking which belongings she wants to keep.
story.punchline: She'd be needing somewhere to sit.
story.script: Twenty dollars. A stranger was measuring it while Joan stood in the doorway with her hospital bag. Her son Paul told the buyer to give them a minute. Joan sat in the chair. The buyer put his tape away. Paul said the stairs weren't safe anymore. His brother had found her a ground-floor flat, and they'd wanted to spare her the difficult sorting. Joan asked why the wedding photographs were in the sale box. Neither son had an answer. Paul said she couldn't take everything. He was right about that, which made her angrier. She'd been asking for help finding a smaller place for months. She hadn't asked them to decide what her life was worth keeping. His brother offered to buy the chair back. Joan asked whom he planned to pay. It was still hers. The buyer quietly said he hadn't handed over any money. Paul tried to announce that the sale would resume after lunch. Joan told him it wouldn't. She asked the buyer whether he still wanted the enormous dining table. He did. That could go. So could the spare beds. Then she took a blank price sticker and wrote RESERVED across it. Paul reached for her hospital bag, assuming she wanted help packing. She handed him the photographs instead and pointed toward the new flat's moving boxes. The sticker went on her husband's chair. She'd be needing somewhere to sit.
story.twist: Her sons mistake needing a smaller home for permission to choose what she should lose, including the chair she still uses to feel close to her late husband.

youtube.description: A mother comes home from hospital to an estate sale she never authorized, and must choose what moving on means for herself.
youtube.title: Twenty Dollars for Her Husband's Chair

story.conflict: An employee who votes against a newer colleague must confront her own complicity when the manager turns anonymous votes into personal blame.
story.hook: Her boss turned a layoff into a popularity vote. He told the newest employee to hand out the ballots.
story.like_cta: LIKE IF THAT WASNT A CHOICE
story.premise: A boss makes employees vote on who should lose their job and orders the newest worker to distribute ballots bearing her own name.
story.script: Nina passed Ruth a pencil, then put a ballot beside it. Her own name was first on the list. Martin said the company needed one less salary. The team could choose fairly, or he'd make the choice himself. He promised the votes would be anonymous. Ruth had a mortgage. Nina had only been there six weeks. Ruth wrote her name and folded the paper before anyone could see. Then Martin pushed the ballot box toward Ruth and told her to read the choices aloud. Nina pulled up a chair to help count. Ruth opened her vote first. Under the name, she'd written that Nina needed more training. Yesterday, Nina had stayed late to teach Ruth the new ordering system. Ruth couldn't make herself read it. Martin told her the team was waiting. So Ruth said she'd voted for Nina, and why. Nina stopped reaching for the papers. Ruth asked to change her vote. Martin said the decision was already made; Nina had the most. He slid a dismissal letter across the table and called it the team's decision. Ruth told him to sign his own name. He did. That didn't give Nina her job back. Ruth followed her to the lockers and offered to carry her things. Nina handed her the pencil instead. Ruth started to explain about the mortgage, then stopped. She hadn't asked whether Nina had one too. Ruth still had her job. Nina didn't owe her forgiveness.
story.twist: The boss's supposedly anonymous team decision requires the voters to confront the person they sacrificed, and regretting a vote does not undo its harm.

youtube.description: A boss calls a layoff vote fair and anonymous, until one employee has to face the colleague she chose.
youtube.title: The Pencil Beside the Layoff Ballot

story.conflict: A cleaner must make an audience understand that her humiliation is real while her employer tries to sell every objection as part of the performance.
story.hook: A cleaner discovered her employer was selling tickets to watch her work. He'd told the guests her mistakes were part of the comedy.
story.like_cta: LIKE IF HE COULD CLEAN IT
story.premise: A wealthy employer sells tickets to watch his cleaner work, misleading guests into thinking she is performing a comedy act.
story.punchline: This time, everyone was looking at him.
story.script: Keira dropped a sponge and six people applauded. She thought they'd mistaken her for somebody else. Then a guest showed her the program: The Hopeless Housekeeper. Fifty dollars a seat. Keira was earning twelve an hour. Her employer, Victor, rang the little silver bell he used when he wanted something cleaned. He'd spilled wine beside his chair. Keira asked why her shift had a ticket price. Victor told the guests her angry face was part of the act. They laughed again. She put down her bucket and said she wasn't an actress. A woman at the table asked whether that was in the script. There wasn't a script. Victor had told Keira he was having friends over for dinner. He tried to send her into the kitchen before she ruined the surprise. The woman asked him what he'd paid Keira to perform. Victor said she was already being paid to work. Nobody laughed. Keira picked up her bucket. Victor warned her there was still a whole dinner to clear. The woman started stacking plates. Another guest brought them to the sink. Victor called that audience participation. Keira said her shift ended at nine, and pointed to the clock. Then she left him the cloth for his wine. As she put on her coat, the woman rang the silver bell. Victor looked toward the empty kitchen doorway. This time, everyone was looking at him.
story.twist: The guests believe they have paid for a consenting performer's show, then stop laughing and help clean when they learn she is an ordinary worker.

youtube.description: Dinner guests think a cleaner is performing a comedy act, until she explains what her employer actually told her.
youtube.title: Fifty Dollars to Watch Her Clean
